title: Capital Structure - Modigliani and Miller Theory, Financial Leverage and Corporate Taxes
description: A highly challenging assessment of capital structure decisions, financial leverage, homemade leverage, Modigliani and Miller propositions, tax shields, cost of equity, firm value and shareholder wealth.
subject: FIN2372 - Advanced Corporate Finance

questions.question: An unlevered firm has a market value of Rs. 1,200 million. Management is considering replacing Rs. 400 million of equity with permanent debt while leaving the firm's operating assets unchanged. If the restructuring increases total firm value to Rs. 1,320 million, what is the value of equity immediately after the restructuring?
options: Rs. 800 million
Rs. 920 million
Rs. 1,080 million
Rs. 1,320 million
questions.answer: Rs. 920 million
questions.rationale: Firm value equals the market value of debt plus equity. With firm value of Rs. 1,320 million and debt of Rs. 400 million, equity is worth Rs. 920 million.

questions.question: A company worth Rs. 1,000 million has no debt and 100 million shares outstanding. It borrows Rs. 500 million and immediately distributes the entire amount as a cash dividend. After the transaction, the total value of the firm is Rs. 1,250 million. Ignoring taxes and transaction costs for this question, what is the total wealth effect experienced by the original shareholders relative to their position before restructuring?
options: A gain of Rs. 250 million
No change in total shareholder wealth
A loss of Rs. 250 million
A gain of Rs. 500 million
questions.answer: A gain of Rs. 250 million
questions.rationale: After restructuring, equity is worth Rs. 750 million because debt is Rs. 500 million. Shareholders also receive Rs. 500 million in dividends, giving total wealth of Rs. 1,250 million compared with the original Rs. 1,000 million.

questions.question: An unlevered company worth Rs. 1,000 million borrows Rs. 500 million and distributes the proceeds to shareholders. Following restructuring, firm value falls to Rs. 750 million. Which statement best describes the resulting effect on the original shareholders?
options: Their wealth is unchanged because every rupee of new debt is received as a dividend
Their wealth rises because leverage always transfers value from creditors to shareholders
Their wealth falls by Rs. 250 million because the reduction in equity value exceeds any financing benefit
Their wealth falls by Rs. 500 million because the entire debt becomes a direct personal liability
questions.answer: Their wealth falls by Rs. 250 million because the reduction in equity value exceeds any financing benefit
questions.rationale: The post restructuring equity value is Rs. 250 million. Adding the Rs. 500 million dividend gives total shareholder wealth of Rs. 750 million, which is Rs. 250 million below the original value.

questions.question: Why should shareholders generally support the capital structure that maximizes total firm value even though their direct claim is only on equity?
options: Any increase in firm value must legally be distributed immediately as a cash dividend
Changes in capital structure benefit shareholders when the resulting increase in total firm value exceeds the associated financing claims
Maximizing firm value guarantees that the market value of outstanding debt will decline
Shareholders receive both the equity value and the full market value of outstanding debt
questions.answer: Changes in capital structure benefit shareholders when the resulting increase in total firm value exceeds the associated financing claims
questions.rationale: A value creating restructuring increases the total economic pie. After recognizing the fixed claim of debt, the additional value generated by the restructuring benefits shareholders.

questions.question: An all equity firm has assets worth Rs. 8,000, 400 shares outstanding and expected EBIT of Rs. 1,200. It considers borrowing Rs. 4,000 at 10 percent and using the proceeds to repurchase 200 shares. Ignoring taxes, what happens to expected earnings per share after restructuring?
options: It increases from Rs. 3 to Rs. 4
It increases from Rs. 3 to Rs. 6
It decreases from Rs. 3 to Rs. 2
It remains at Rs. 3 because firm value is unchanged
questions.answer: It increases from Rs. 3 to Rs. 4
questions.rationale: Without debt, expected earnings per share are Rs. 1,200 divided by 400 shares, or Rs. 3. With debt, interest is Rs. 400, leaving Rs. 800 for 200 shares, producing earnings per share of Rs. 4.

questions.question: Using the same firm with Rs. 4,000 of debt at 10 percent and 200 shares after restructuring, EBIT falls to Rs. 400 during a recession. Ignoring taxes, which comparison between the levered and unlevered structures is correct?
options: Levered earnings per share are zero while unlevered earnings per share are Rs. 1
Levered earnings per share are Rs. 1 while unlevered earnings per share are zero
Both structures produce earnings per share of Rs. 1 because total assets are unchanged
Levered earnings per share are negative because interest exceeds EBIT
questions.answer: Levered earnings per share are zero while unlevered earnings per share are Rs. 1
questions.rationale: Under leverage, the entire Rs. 400 EBIT is absorbed by interest, leaving zero for shareholders. Without debt, Rs. 400 divided by 400 shares gives earnings per share of Rs. 1.

questions.question: For a firm considering leverage, the earnings per share lines for the levered and unlevered capital structures intersect at a particular EBIT level. What is the most accurate interpretation of this point?
options: It is the EBIT level at which the firm's total market value must equal zero
It is the EBIT level at which shareholders receive the same earnings per share under either capital structure
It is the EBIT level at which interest expense becomes equal to the market value of debt
It is the EBIT level above which the unlevered structure always produces greater earnings per share
questions.answer: It is the EBIT level at which shareholders receive the same earnings per share under either capital structure
questions.rationale: The break even EBIT is the operating income level at which the earnings per share produced by the levered and unlevered financing alternatives are identical.

questions.question: A firm has 400 shares under an unlevered structure. Alternatively, it can borrow Rs. 4,000 at 10 percent and reduce the number of shares to 200. Ignoring taxes, at what EBIT level will earnings per share be identical under both structures?
questions.rationale: At EBIT of Rs. 800, the unlevered firm earns Rs. 2 per share. The levered firm pays Rs. 400 interest and distributes the remaining Rs. 400 across 200 shares, also producing Rs. 2 per share.

questions.question: Why does financial leverage magnify both favorable and unfavorable outcomes for shareholders even when the firm's operating assets remain unchanged?
options: Debt causes operating income itself to become more volatile across economic states
Fixed interest claims leave a more variable residual cash flow to be distributed across a smaller equity base
Debt holders participate proportionately in all increases and decreases in residual earnings
Leverage guarantees a higher return on equity whenever the firm reports positive EBIT
questions.answer: Fixed interest claims leave a more variable residual cash flow to be distributed across a smaller equity base
questions.rationale: Debt introduces a fixed financing obligation. Changes in EBIT therefore produce proportionately larger changes in the residual earnings and returns available to equity holders.

questions.question: Under Modigliani and Miller Proposition I without taxes, a firm replaces part of its equity with debt while its investment policy and operating cash flows remain unchanged. Which outcome is theoretically required?
options: Firm value rises because debt is always less expensive than equity
Firm value falls because leverage necessarily increases financial risk
Firm value remains unchanged because financing merely reallocates operating cash flows among investors
Firm value rises until the cost of debt becomes equal to the cost of equity
questions.answer: Firm value remains unchanged because financing merely reallocates operating cash flows among investors
questions.rationale: Under the assumptions of Modigliani and Miller without taxes, capital structure does not change the total operating cash flow generated by assets and therefore cannot change total firm value.

questions.question: Which assumption is most essential to the homemade leverage argument supporting Modigliani and Miller Proposition I?
options: Individual investors must be able to borrow and lend on terms comparable to those available to firms
Corporate managers must always prefer debt financing to equity financing
Debt must have a higher required return than equity at every leverage level
All companies must maintain identical debt to equity ratios within an industry
questions.answer: Individual investors must be able to borrow and lend on terms comparable to those available to firms
questions.rationale: Homemade leverage requires investors to replicate or reverse corporate leverage personally. This depends critically on comparable borrowing and lending opportunities.

questions.question: A levered firm's securities become overpriced relative to an otherwise identical unlevered firm in a perfect capital market. Which investor action is most consistent with the homemade leverage argument?
options: Buy the overpriced levered equity because its earnings per share are necessarily higher
Replicate the levered payoff using the cheaper unlevered equity combined with personal borrowing
Buy only the firm's debt because debt always captures the entire arbitrage profit
Avoid both firms because equivalent operating assets cannot support different financing arrangements
questions.answer: Replicate the levered payoff using the cheaper unlevered equity combined with personal borrowing
questions.rationale: If equivalent payoffs can be created more cheaply through personal borrowing and unlevered equity, investors will prefer that strategy and arbitrage should eliminate the valuation difference.

questions.question: Under Modigliani and Miller Proposition I without taxes, why does increasing the proportion of apparently cheaper debt fail to reduce the firm's overall cost of capital?
options: The cost of debt automatically increases by exactly the same percentage as the debt ratio
The required return on equity rises as leverage increases, offsetting the greater use of cheaper debt
The market value of equity remains fixed regardless of the amount of debt issued
The operating risk of the firm's assets falls sufficiently to neutralize the financing benefit
questions.answer: The required return on equity rises as leverage increases, offsetting the greater use of cheaper debt
questions.rationale: Under Modigliani and Miller without taxes, greater leverage increases equity risk and therefore the required return on equity, keeping the weighted average cost of capital constant.

questions.question: An unlevered firm has a required return of 15 percent. Its debt costs 9 percent and its debt to equity ratio is 0.5. Under Modigliani and Miller Proposition II without taxes, what required return should shareholders demand on the levered equity?
options: 15 percent
17 percent
18 percent
21 percent
questions.answer: 18 percent
questions.rationale: The leverage premium is 0.5 multiplied by the 6 percentage point difference between the unlevered return and debt cost, giving 3 percentage points. The levered equity return is therefore 18 percent.

questions.question: A firm operating in a no tax Modigliani and Miller world has an unlevered cost of capital of 14 percent and debt costing 8 percent. If its debt to equity ratio rises from 0.5 to 1.5, what is the most accurate consequence?
options: The cost of equity rises from 17 percent to 23 percent while the overall cost of capital remains 14 percent
The cost of equity rises from 14 percent to 20 percent while the overall cost of capital falls to 11 percent
The cost of equity remains 14 percent because capital structure cannot affect investor risk
The cost of equity rises from 17 percent to 20 percent while the overall cost of capital rises to 17 percent
questions.answer: The cost of equity rises from 17 percent to 23 percent while the overall cost of capital remains 14 percent
questions.rationale: At a debt to equity ratio of 0.5, the equity return is 17 percent. At 1.5, the leverage premium is 9 percentage points, producing 23 percent. Proposition I keeps the overall cost of capital at 14 percent.

questions.question: Which change would most directly undermine the conclusion that levered and unlevered firms must have identical values under the original Modigliani and Miller Proposition I?
options: Investors develop different preferences for receiving dividends at different dates
Interest payments become deductible for corporate tax purposes while equity distributions are not
A company changes the number of shares outstanding without changing its financing mix
Managers disclose the same operating information simultaneously to all investors
questions.answer: Interest payments become deductible for corporate tax purposes while equity distributions are not
questions.rationale: Corporate tax deductibility creates an additional cash flow benefit from debt, breaking the capital structure irrelevance result of the no tax model.

questions.question: A permanent debt issue of Rs. 600 million carries an interest rate of 8 percent. The corporate tax rate is 30 percent. Assuming the standard perpetual debt assumptions, what is the present value of the interest tax shield?
options: Rs. 14.4 million
Rs. 48 million
Rs. 180 million
Rs. 600 million
questions.answer: Rs. 180 million
questions.rationale: Under permanent debt, the present value of the tax shield equals the corporate tax rate multiplied by the amount of debt. Thirty percent of Rs. 600 million is Rs. 180 million.

questions.question: An unlevered firm is worth Rs. 900 million. It permanently introduces Rs. 300 million of debt in a world with a 25 percent corporate tax rate and no bankruptcy costs. According to Modigliani and Miller Proposition I with corporate taxes, what is the value of the levered firm?
options: Rs. 975 million
Rs. 1,125 million
Rs. 1,200 million
Rs. 825 million
questions.answer: Rs. 975 million
questions.rationale: The value added by the permanent tax shield is 25 percent of Rs. 300 million, or Rs. 75 million. Adding this to the unlevered value gives Rs. 975 million.

questions.question: A firm generates perpetual EBIT of Rs. 200 million. Its corporate tax rate is 25 percent and the required return on an equivalent unlevered firm is 15 percent. What is the value of the unlevered firm?
options: Rs. 1,000 million
Rs. 1,333.33 million
Rs. 750 million
Rs. 1,500 million
questions.answer: Rs. 1,000 million
questions.rationale: After tax operating cash flow is Rs. 150 million. Capitalizing this perpetual cash flow at 15 percent gives an unlevered firm value of Rs. 1,000 million.

questions.question: The firm in the previous scenario introduces Rs. 400 million of permanent debt while retaining the same operating assets. The corporate tax rate remains 25 percent. Under Modigliani and Miller with corporate taxes, what are the new firm value and equity value respectively?
options: Rs. 1,000 million and Rs. 600 million
Rs. 1,100 million and Rs. 700 million
Rs. 1,400 million and Rs. 1,000 million
Rs. 1,100 million and Rs. 1,100 million
questions.answer: Rs. 1,100 million and Rs. 700 million
questions.rationale: The tax shield adds Rs. 100 million to the Rs. 1,000 million unlevered value. The levered firm is therefore worth Rs. 1,100 million, leaving Rs. 700 million of equity after subtracting Rs. 400 million of debt.

questions.question: A company has an unlevered cost of capital of 20 percent, debt costing 10 percent, a corporate tax rate of 30 percent and a debt to equity ratio of 0.5. Under Modigliani and Miller Proposition II with corporate taxes, what is the required return on levered equity?
options: 22.5 percent
23.5 percent
25 percent
27 percent
questions.answer: 23.5 percent
questions.rationale: The leverage premium equals 0.5 multiplied by 70 percent multiplied by the 10 percentage point difference between the unlevered return and debt cost. This adds 3.5 percentage points to the 20 percent unlevered return.

questions.question: Two otherwise identical firms differ only in capital structure. Firm U is entirely equity financed, while Firm L uses permanent debt. Corporate taxes exist, but bankruptcy costs and other market imperfections do not. Why should Firm L have a higher total value?
options: Debt reduces the operating risk of the firm's underlying assets
Debt causes shareholders to accept a lower required return despite greater financial risk
Interest deductibility creates additional after tax cash flow available collectively to investors
Debt financing increases EBIT because interest expense is recorded below operating income
questions.answer: Interest deductibility creates additional after tax cash flow available collectively to investors
questions.rationale: The tax deduction on interest reduces corporate taxes and creates an additional cash flow equal to the interest tax shield, increasing total firm value.

questions.question: A levered firm has EBIT of Rs. 2,000, debt of Rs. 8,000 carrying 8 percent interest and a corporate tax rate of 35 percent. What is the total cash flow distributed to shareholders and bondholders combined?
questions.rationale: Interest is Rs. 640. Taxable income is Rs. 1,360 and taxes are Rs. 476. Shareholders receive Rs. 884 and bondholders receive Rs. 640, producing total investor cash flow of Rs. 1,524.

questions.question: An otherwise identical unlevered firm generates EBIT of Rs. 2,000 and faces a corporate tax rate of 35 percent. A levered version has Rs. 8,000 of debt at 8 percent. By how much does leverage increase annual total cash flow to investors?
questions.rationale: The annual tax shield equals the interest expense of Rs. 640 multiplied by the 35 percent tax rate, giving Rs. 224 of additional cash flow.

questions.question: Under Modigliani and Miller with corporate taxes, which statement best explains why the increase in the cost of equity caused by leverage is smaller than under the corresponding no tax model?
options: Corporate taxes eliminate the fixed contractual obligation associated with debt
The tax shield absorbs part of the leverage effect reflected in the relationship between debt and equity risk
The government guarantees a portion of shareholder returns whenever debt is issued
Corporate taxes cause the required return on unlevered assets to decline automatically
questions.answer: The tax shield absorbs part of the leverage effect reflected in the relationship between debt and equity risk
questions.rationale: The corporate tax adjustment reduces the leverage premium incorporated into the required return on equity relative to the no tax Modigliani and Miller relationship.

questions.question: A company increases permanent debt while operating risk remains unchanged. Under Modigliani and Miller with corporate taxes and no bankruptcy costs, which combination of effects is theoretically expected?
options: Firm value decreases, equity risk decreases and the weighted average cost of capital increases
Firm value increases, equity required return increases and the weighted average cost of capital tends to decrease
Firm value remains constant, equity required return remains constant and the weighted average cost of capital decreases
Firm value increases, equity required return decreases and the cost of debt becomes equal to the unlevered return
questions.answer: Firm value increases, equity required return increases and the weighted average cost of capital tends to decrease
questions.rationale: The interest tax shield increases firm value and creates a financing advantage, while greater financial leverage still increases the risk and required return of equity.

questions.question: The basic Modigliani and Miller model with corporate taxes and no bankruptcy costs appears to imply that firms should use extremely high levels of debt. What feature of the model produces this implication?
options: The model assumes debt reduces operating risk continuously as borrowing increases
The model recognizes the tax benefit of debt but excludes major offsetting costs associated with excessive leverage
The model assumes shareholders never require additional return when financial leverage increases
The model assumes the tax shield declines as the amount of permanent debt increases
questions.answer: The model recognizes the tax benefit of debt but excludes major offsetting costs associated with excessive leverage
questions.rationale: If each additional unit of permanent debt creates tax shield value while no bankruptcy or distress costs are recognized, the simplified model gives debt a continuing valuation advantage.

questions.question: Suppose a firm's cost of debt is below its unlevered cost of capital. A manager argues that replacing equity with cheaper debt must continuously reduce the overall cost of capital even in a no tax perfect market. What is the key flaw in this argument?
options: It ignores the increase in the required return on the remaining equity as financial leverage rises
It assumes debt holders receive interest before shareholders receive residual earnings
It incorrectly assumes that equity holders have a residual claim on operating cash flows
It ignores the fact that the cost of debt must always exceed the unlevered cost of capital
questions.answer: It ignores the increase in the required return on the remaining equity as financial leverage rises
questions.rationale: The apparent advantage of using cheaper debt is exactly offset in the no tax Modigliani and Miller framework by the rising required return on increasingly risky equity.

questions.question: An investor owns equity in an unlevered company but wants the higher financial exposure associated with the levered version of an otherwise identical company. In a perfect capital market, which strategy most directly creates homemade leverage?
options: Borrow personally and invest the borrowed funds together with personal wealth in the unlevered equity
Lend part of personal wealth and invest the remainder in the unlevered equity
Purchase corporate bonds and finance them entirely by selling unlevered shares
Hold additional cash while maintaining the same investment in the unlevered equity
questions.answer: Borrow personally and invest the borrowed funds together with personal wealth in the unlevered equity
questions.rationale: Personal borrowing allows an investor to magnify exposure to unlevered equity and replicate the financial leverage that would otherwise be created at the corporate level.

questions.question: An investor owns shares in a highly levered firm but prefers the payoff pattern of an equivalent unlevered investment. Under the assumptions supporting capital structure irrelevance, which strategy best offsets the firm's leverage?
options: Borrow personally and purchase additional shares in the levered firm
Sell part of the levered equity investment and lend the appropriate amount personally
Purchase additional corporate debt while retaining the entire levered equity position
Use dividend income to purchase more levered equity whenever EBIT decreases
questions.answer: Sell part of the levered equity investment and lend the appropriate amount personally
questions.rationale: Investors can undo corporate leverage by reducing exposure to levered equity and personally lending funds, allowing them to replicate a less levered payoff pattern.

questions.question: A company has an unlevered value of Rs. 2,000 million and permanent debt of Rs. 800 million. Its corporate tax rate rises unexpectedly from 20 percent to 30 percent while all operating cash flows and financing arrangements remain unchanged. Under Modigliani and Miller with corporate taxes, by how much should firm value increase?
options: Rs. 40 million
Rs. 80 million
Rs. 160 million
Rs. 240 million
questions.answer: Rs. 80 million
questions.rationale: The additional tax shield value equals the 10 percentage point increase in the corporate tax rate multiplied by Rs. 800 million of permanent debt, producing Rs. 80 million.

questions.question: An unlevered firm has a market value of Rs. 1,500 million. It introduces Rs. 600 million of permanent debt in a country with a 30 percent corporate tax rate. Immediately after restructuring, what proportion of the levered firm's total value is represented by equity under the Modigliani and Miller tax model?
options: Approximately 46.4 percent
Approximately 64.3 percent
Approximately 71.4 percent
Approximately 82.1 percent
questions.answer: Approximately 64.3 percent
questions.rationale: The tax shield is Rs. 180 million, making firm value Rs. 1,680 million. Equity is therefore Rs. 1,080 million, which represents approximately 64.3 percent of total firm value.

questions.question: A firm has an unlevered required return of 16 percent, debt costing 8 percent, a corporate tax rate of 25 percent and a debt to equity ratio of 2. Under Modigliani and Miller Proposition II with taxes, what is the required return on equity?
options: 24 percent
26 percent
28 percent
32 percent
questions.answer: 28 percent
questions.rationale: The leverage premium is 2 multiplied by 75 percent multiplied by the 8 percentage point spread between the unlevered return and debt cost. This produces a 12 percentage point premium and a 28 percent required return on equity.

questions.question: Consider two firms with identical operating assets and perpetual EBIT. Firm L uses debt while Firm U is entirely equity financed. In a world with corporate taxes, which cash flow comparison most directly explains the difference in their values?
options: Firm L generates higher EBIT because interest payments reduce the operating cost of its assets
Firm L provides investors with the same after tax operating cash flow as Firm U plus the benefit generated by the interest tax shield
Firm L transfers all corporate taxes to bondholders, leaving shareholders with tax free residual income
Firm L generates a higher pre interest operating cash flow because debt holders require fixed payments
questions.answer: Firm L provides investors with the same after tax operating cash flow as Firm U plus the benefit generated by the interest tax shield
questions.rationale: The underlying assets generate the same operating cash flows, but interest deductibility creates an additional tax shield cash flow for the levered firm.

questions.question: A financial manager observes that leverage increases earnings per share in the expected and expansion scenarios but decreases earnings per share in a recession. The manager concludes that the levered structure must therefore maximize shareholder wealth. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: The conclusion is valid because a higher expected earnings per share necessarily implies a higher market value of equity
The conclusion is incomplete because earnings per share effects alone ignore changes in risk, required returns, taxes and total firm value
The conclusion is valid because leverage always increases shareholder wealth whenever expected EBIT exceeds interest expense
The conclusion is incorrect only because shareholders are concerned exclusively with return on equity rather than earnings per share
questions.answer: The conclusion is incomplete because earnings per share effects alone ignore changes in risk, required returns, taxes and total firm value
questions.rationale: A capital structure cannot be judged solely by its effect on earnings per share. Shareholder wealth depends on the value of the underlying cash flows after considering risk, financing effects and the resulting total value of the firm.
